diagnostic_evidence.quote: If rows $j$ and $k$ are conjugate pair of complex rows in $\matM$ with $j<k$, and $\gamma_k\gamma_l\neq0$ then

issues.failure_explanation: The lemma's statement (the weak inverse is real) is correct, but its proof in Section sec:proof-winv-realness is invalid. (i) The four ring equations claimed for the constructed real candidate y state the last two with the entrywise pseudoinverse, (a ⋆_M y)^pinv = a ⋆_M y, which is false in general (e.g. M = [[1,1],[1,-1]], a = (1,1) gives a ⋆_M a^winv = (1/2,1/2), whose entrywise pseudoinverse is (2,2)); the Moore-Penrose-type conditions require the ring conjugate ^sconj, as in Lemma lem:added-2. (ii) The construction of y omits the case γ_j = γ_k = 0 for a complex conjugate row pair (and states its condition with an undefined index l), so y is not defined for all a. (iii) Fatally, the concluding step asserts that R_y and R_{a^winv} are Moore-Penrose pseudoinverses of R_a and invokes Moore-Penrose uniqueness. This is false for general M: the ring conjugation corresponds to the matrix Hermitian adjoint of representation matrices only when M M^H is diagonal; in general R_{a^winv} = M^{-1} diag((Ma)^pinv) M is the group inverse of the (non-normal) matrix R_a, not its Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse (e.g. M = [[1,2],[3,5]], a = M^{-1}(1,0)^T gives R_{a^winv} = R_a = [[-5,-10],[3,6]] while R_a^+ = (1/170)[[-5,3],[-10,6]]). Hence the uniqueness argument does not apply.

failure_location.quote: The same four equation hold if we replace $\va$ with $\matR_\va$, $\vy$ with $\matR_\vy$ and $\Mprod$ with matrix product. Thus, $\matR_\vy$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\matR_\va$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the Moore-Penrose detour with the direct structural argument: conjugation commutes with entrywise inversion, so (Ma)^pinv inherits the real-entry/conjugate-pair structure of Ma, and a^winv = M^{-1}(Ma)^pinv is real by Lemma lem:struct-Minv (the same argument already used for the realness of the ⋆_M-product). Equivalently, correct ^pinv to ^sconj, add the missing zero case to the construction of y, and conclude y = a^winv via the uniqueness in Lemma lem:added-2.
issues.overall_effect: As written the paper does not validly prove that the weak inverse is real; consequently the membership claim a^winv ∈ K_M inside Lemma lem:added-2 (and hence that lemma's statement of unique weak inverses in K_M) is also unestablished by the given arguments. The underlying statements are true, so nothing downstream is lost once the proof is repaired.
issues.title: Invalid Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse argument in the deferred proof of Lemma lem:winv-realness
issues.why_classification: The statement is true and the repair is a short, local argument built entirely from results already proved in the paper (Lemma lem:struct-Minv, or the uniqueness in Lemma lem:added-2); every affected claim, including Lemma lem:added-2, survives unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Up to isomorphism, every commutative ring over $\R^2$ is isomorphic to one of three possible rings: complex numbers, split-complex numbers and dual numbers~\cite{jaglom-1968-complex}. We already seen that the first is a tubal ring.
The rings $\KM$ and ${\mathbb{K}}_{\matM'}$ are isomorphic if their realness is the same.

issues.failure_explanation: The text claims there are exactly ⌈n/2⌉ tubal rings up to isomorphism. The realness m can be any integer in {0,...,n} having the same parity as n, which gives ⌊n/2⌋+1 isomorphism classes (via the canonical rings K_{n,m} ≅ R^m × C^{(n-m)/2}). For even n the stated count is off by one: for n = 2 it yields 1, while the paper's own examples exhibit two non-isomorphic tubal rings over R^2, the complex numbers (realness 0) and the split-complex numbers (realness 2). The claim is additionally underjustified: an exact count requires that different realness values give non-isomorphic rings, but Proposition prop:realness-iso is stated and proved only in the 'if' direction.

failure_location.quote: Since complex rows in $\matM$ come in pairs, the parity of the realness must be equal to the parity of $n$, thus there are, up to isomorphism, $\lceil \nicefrac{n}{2} \rceil$ tubal rings.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace ⌈n/2⌉ with ⌊n/2⌋+1 and add the standard observation that realness is an isomorphism invariant (e.g. K_{n,m} is isomorphic as a real algebra to R^m × C^{(n-m)/2}, from which m is recoverable), upgrading Proposition prop:realness-iso to 'if and only if'.
issues.overall_effect: The enumeration of tubal rings up to isomorphism is wrong for every even n and directly contradicts the n = 2 examples in the same section; it is a standalone remark and is not used by later results.
issues.title: Incorrect count of tubal rings up to isomorphism
issues.why_classification: The fix is a corrected counting formula plus a short standard invariance remark; no theorem, construction, or algorithm in the paper depends on this count, so all substantive claims survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: This clearly defines a commutative ring over $\R^2$. Furthermore, it can be verified that weak inverses for non-zero elements are given by:

issues.failure_explanation: For the split-complex product (M = [[1,1],[1,-1]]) the generic weak-inverse formula [a/(a²-b²); -b/(a²-b²)] is valid exactly when a² ≠ b². Stating it '(for a≠b)' leaves it undefined whenever a = -b ≠ 0 (e.g. (a,b) = (1,-1) produces division by zero), and the companion special case on the line a = -b, namely [a;-a]^winv = [1/(4a); -1/(4a)], is missing — only [a;a]^winv = [1/(4a); 1/(4a)] is given. As written, the displayed formulas fail on a one-dimensional subset of the non-zero elements they claim to cover.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the generic formula under the condition a² ≠ b² (equivalently a ≠ ±b) and add the missing case [a;-a]^winv = [1/(4a); -1/(4a)] for a ≠ 0.
issues.overall_effect: Within an illustrative example, the displayed weak-inverse formulas are incorrect/incomplete on the line a = -b; the example's conclusion that the split-complex numbers form a tubal ring is unaffected, since weak inverses exist by the general theory.
issues.title: Split-complex weak-inverse formulas use the wrong generic condition and omit the a = -b case
issues.why_classification: The repair is a local correction of a case condition plus the omitted case inside an example; no result or guarantee elsewhere in the paper depends on these formulas.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then there exist $\Mprod$-unitary tensors $\tenU \in \KM^{m\times m}$ and $\tenV \in \KM^{p\times p}$ and an f-diagonal tensor $\tenS \in \KM^{m\times p}$ such that $\tenA = \tenU \Mprod \tenS \Mprod \tenV^\ha$.
We can then move back to the primal domain to obtain $\tenA = \tenU \Mprod \tenS \Mprod \tenV^\ha$.
every row of $\matM$ is either real, or obtained by entry-wise complex conjugation of exactly one other row of $\matM$

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem asserts U ∈ K_M^{m×m} and V ∈ K_M^{p×p}, i.e. real tensors. Because M's complex rows come in conjugate pairs, the faces of Â satisfy Â_k = conj(Â_j) on each conjugate pair (and are real on real faces). The inverse transform of Û is real only if Û has the same conjugate-pair structure, which requires choosing the per-face SVD factors consistently — e.g. the SVD of Â_k taken as the entrywise conjugate of the SVD of Â_j. The proof instead constructs 'a SVD decomposition for each frontal slice on its own'; since SVD factors are not unique, independent per-face choices generically break the pairing, and 'moving back to the primal domain' then yields non-real U and V, outside K_M. This consistency step is necessary and is missing (Ŝ is unaffected because paired faces have identical singular values, which is why S stays real).

failure_location.quote: Construct a SVD decomposition for each frontal slices on its own, collecting the left and right unitary matrices to form $\hat{\tenU}$ and $\hat{\tenV}$ respectively, and the singular values in $\hat{\tenS}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Stipulate that on each conjugate face pair the SVD of Â_k is chosen as the entrywise conjugate of the SVD of Â_j (possible because Â_k = conj(Â_j)), and a real SVD on each real face; then Û and V̂ have the required conjugate structure and U, V are real, completing the proof without changing any statement.
issues.overall_effect: As written, the construction may output non-real factors, so the existence of the ⋆_M-SVD within K_M is not fully established; the truncated-SVD optimality proofs (Theorems thm:first-eckart-young and thm:second-eckart-young), which build truncations from this facewise SVD, inherit the same gap.
issues.title: Proof of the ⋆_M-SVD does not ensure the unitary factors are real tensors
issues.why_classification: The statement is true and the missing step is a standard, contained consistency choice for the per-face SVDs; the repair adds no new lemma and leaves the SVD theorem and all dependent optimality results intact.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\lrapprox{\tenA}{\vr}$ is the the optimal $\Mprod$-multirank-$k$ approximation of $\tenA$ in the Frobenius norm.
every row of $\matM$ is either real, or obtained by entry-wise complex conjugation of exactly one other row of $\matM$

issues.failure_explanation: For a real tensor A the transformed faces obey Â_k = conj(Â_j) on each conjugate row-pair of M, so every real competitor B has equal face-ranks on the pair. The theorem, however, admits an arbitrary tuple r ≤ Mmultirank(A) and truncates face j at rank r_j. If r_j ≠ r_k on a conjugate pair (e.g. the t-product with n = 3 and r = (1,1,0), which is allowed whenever Mmultirank(A) ≥ (1,1,1)), the truncated faces are not conjugates, so the constructed [A]_r is not a real tensor: it lies outside K_M^{m×p}, and no real multirank-≤r tensor attains its error (a real competitor is forced to rank min(r_j, r_k) on the pair). Hence, for such r, [A]_r is not 'the optimal multirank-r approximation of A' within the tubal tensor space as the statement claims; only the bare error inequality against real competitors, which follows from per-face Eckart-Young, remains valid. The statement relies on the omitted hypothesis that r be constant on conjugate face pairs (together with conjugate-consistent truncation choices).

failure_location.quote: For any $n$-size tuple of non-negative integers $\vr$ such that $\vr \leq \Mmultirank(\tenA)$, we define the tensor $\lrapprox{\tenA}{\vr}$ as the tensor in which the frontal domain $j$ in the transformed space is the $r_j$ truncated SVD of the $j$th frontal face of the transformed $\tenA$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the statement to tuples r that are constant on each conjugate face-pair (equivalently, multirank patterns of real tensors) and choose the paired truncations as conjugates; then [A]_r is real and is the true optimal multirank-≤r approximation in K_M^{m×p}.
issues.overall_effect: For pair-inconsistent multirank tuples the constructed 'optimal approximation' is not an element of the real tensor space and is not the constrained optimum there; the theorem's approximation guarantee is reliable exactly in the pair-consistent regime (the one arising in practice), while for inconsistent tuples only the inequality ‖A - [A]_r‖ ≤ ‖A - B‖ survives.
issues.title: Multirank Eckart-Young theorem admits truncation tuples whose truncation is not a real tensor
issues.why_classification: Any faithful repair narrows the theorem's quantified domain (excluding pair-inconsistent tuples, for which the named optimizer provably leaves the tensor space) or abandons the in-space optimality reading; this is a genuine but limited weakening — the Eckart-Young guarantee and rates survive in the natural regime — so it is more than a routine patch but requires no new global proof architecture.

We would expect that this adjoint will be given by the conjugate to $\va$, i.e., $T^\adj_\va(\vy)=T_{\va^\sconj}(\vy)=\va^\sconj \Mprod \vy$, however it is easy to build counter examples for which this does not hold.

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition asserts ⟨A ⋆_M X, Y⟩_F = ⟨X, A^H ⋆_M Y⟩_F for every A ∈ K_M^{m×p} with no hypothesis on M. Its proof reduces the identity tube-wise to Proposition prop:hilbert-algebra, which establishes the key step only under the hypothesis M = D W with D a real invertible diagonal matrix and W unitary. Without that hypothesis the statement is false: the paper itself notes that for general M one can build counterexamples to the underlying adjoint identity. The hypothesis on M is simply missing from the statement.
